admin.name: Managing everyday admin and repetitive tasks

tasks.t: Sorting and replying to routine emails
tasks.fix: Turn the emails you answer most often into reply templates you can reuse.
steps: Find five emails you answer again and again, and remove personal details.
Use the prompt to turn them into reply templates.
Save each template in your email so it is one click away.
tasks.prompt: Here are five emails I answer often, with personal details removed: [paste]. For each one, write a reusable reply template. Put anything that changes each time in [square brackets]. Keep each under 120 words and end with one clear next step.

tasks.t: Booking meetings and moving calendar slots
tasks.fix: Send one booking link instead of trading emails about times.
steps: Block out the times you are free each week.
Turn on a booking page in your calendar, or use a scheduling tool.
Add the link to your email signature and save the reply below as a template.
tasks.template:
Hi [name],

Thanks for getting in touch. To save going back and forth, you can pick a time that suits you here: [booking link]

If none of those times work, just reply and we will find another.

[Your name]
[Business name]

tasks.t: Typing the same details into more than one place
tasks.fix: Collect information once, in one place, and stop retyping it.
steps: Write down where the information starts and everywhere you retype it.
Replace the first step with a form that saves to a sheet.
Use the prompt to see which of your tools can connect directly.
tasks.prompt: I copy this information by hand: [what it is]. It starts in [tool] and I retype it into [tool] and [tool]. In plain English, explain the simplest ways to stop retyping it, starting with options inside tools I already use. Say clearly where you are not sure a feature exists.

tasks.t: Writing up meeting notes and actions
tasks.fix: Turn rough notes into a clean summary in two minutes.
steps: Jot rough notes during the meeting.
Paste them into the prompt.
Check the actions, then send.
tasks.prompt: Turn these rough meeting notes into a three-line summary, the decisions made, and a list of actions with owner and date. Use only what is in the notes. Mark anything unclear with [check]. Notes: [paste notes].

tasks.t: Searching for files you know you saved somewhere
tasks.fix: Set up one simple folder system that everyone uses.
steps: Agree five to seven main folders.
Name every file the same way: date, client, document.
Use the prompt to design the structure for your business.
tasks.prompt: Design a simple shared folder structure for my business. We have [number] people and mainly store [list]. No more than seven main folders. Include one file naming rule and an example file name for each folder.

tasks.t: Repeatedly explaining the same tasks to your team
tasks.fix: Write it down once as a simple SOP (a step-by-step guide), so others can follow it without asking you.
steps: Pick one job people often ask you about.
Jot the steps down, or talk them through, while you do it.
Use the prompt to turn your notes into a checklist.
tasks.prompt: Turn these rough notes on how we do [job] into a step-by-step checklist someone new could follow. Number the steps, flag any step that needs a decision, and mark anything unclear with [check]. Notes: [paste notes].

marketing.name: Creating marketing content and social posts

tasks.t: Coming up with and writing social posts
tasks.fix: Plan a month of posts in one sitting instead of starting from scratch each time.
steps: Pick three questions your customers often ask.
Use the prompt to draft a month of posts.
Edit them to sound like you, then schedule them.
tasks.prompt: Customers often ask: [three questions]. Write eight short social posts, one idea each: four tips, two stories I can fill in and two common mistakes. No more than three hashtags each. Do not make up statistics.

tasks.t: Reusing a blog, talk or video across other channels
tasks.fix: Turn one thing you have already written into a week of content.
steps: Pick one blog, talk or long post.
Paste it into the prompt.
Choose the best versions and schedule them.
tasks.prompt: Here is something I wrote: [paste]. Turn it into three short social posts, one email introduction and five one-line quotes. Use only ideas from the original and keep my wording where you can.

tasks.t: Replying to reviews and comments
tasks.fix: Get a draft reply in seconds, but always send it yourself.
steps: Paste the review or comment into the prompt.
Read the draft and adjust anything personal.
Send it yourself. Never let a reply go out unchecked.
tasks.prompt: Draft a reply to this customer review: [paste]. Thank them, answer their point honestly, and offer one next step if they were unhappy. Under 80 words. Do not promise anything I have not confirmed.

tasks.t: Writing your email newsletter
tasks.fix: Use a fixed template so each issue takes minutes to fill.
steps: Agree three regular sections, such as a tip, news and an offer.
Collect notes during the month.
Use the prompt to turn your notes into the issue.
tasks.prompt: Write my monthly newsletter from these notes: [paste]. Sections: [section 1], [section 2], [section 3]. Give three subject line options. Under 300 words. Do not add facts that are not in my notes.

tasks.t: Reviewing which posts and campaigns got results
tasks.fix: Check a few key numbers each month, then do more of what brought enquiries.
steps: Export last month's post results.
Paste them into the prompt.
Do more of what worked best and drop what worked least.
tasks.prompt: Here are last month's post results: [paste]. Tell me the two posts that did best and the two that did worst, and what each pair has in common. Five bullet points at most. Use only the numbers I gave you.

tasks.t: Drafting detailed replies to clients
tasks.fix: Let AI write the first draft, then you polish it.
steps: Find two or three emails you are happy with.
Paste them into the prompt with the key points for the new email.
Check the facts, then send.
tasks.prompt: Here are emails I have written that sound like me: [paste two or three]. Now write an email to [who] about [topic]. Key points: [list]. Match my tone and length. Do not add facts I have not given you.

tasks.t: Putting together proposals and quotes
tasks.fix: Build your proposal structure once, then fill it from your call notes.
steps: Take your best past proposal and remove the client details.
Paste it into the prompt with your new call notes.
Check every price and date yourself before sending.
tasks.prompt: Here is the structure of a proposal I have used before, with client details removed: [paste]. Here are my notes from a call with a new client: [paste]. Draft a proposal in the same structure. Leave every price and date as [to confirm]. List any questions I should answer before sending.

tasks.t: Preparing reports and client documents
tasks.fix: Give every report the same headings and let AI draft from your notes.
steps: Decide your standard headings.
Paste your notes into the prompt.
Check it and add your own judgement.
tasks.prompt: Turn these notes into a client report with these headings: [list]. Notes: [paste]. Mark anything you are unsure about with [check].

tasks.t: Recreating standard letters and emails each time
tasks.fix: Save each repeated letter once, as a template with blanks.
steps: List the letters you send more than once a month.
Use the prompt to turn each one into a template.
Save them where you write your emails.
tasks.prompt: Turn this letter into a reusable template. Replace anything that changes each time with [square brackets]. Letter: [paste].

tasks.t: Proofreading and tidying the layout before sending
tasks.fix: Ask AI to check your writing against your own rules.
steps: Write three to five house rules, such as British spelling.
Paste the rules and your text into the prompt.
Accept only the changes you agree with.
tasks.prompt: Proofread this text. My rules: [your rules]. Fix spelling, grammar and consistency only. Do not change my meaning. List your changes. Text: [paste].

data.name: Working with spreadsheets and business data

tasks.t: Typing data into spreadsheets by hand
tasks.fix: Let people fill in a form that writes straight into the sheet.
steps: List the columns you fill in by hand.
Make a form with one question per column. Google Forms and Microsoft Forms can both save to a spreadsheet.
Share the form instead of the sheet.
tasks.prompt: I fill in this spreadsheet by hand. The columns are: [list]. The information comes from [where]. Suggest the simplest way to stop typing it in, starting with tools I already use: [list]. Say where you are not sure.

tasks.t: Building weekly or monthly reports
tasks.fix: Build the report once, then just refresh the numbers.
steps: Pick the five numbers you actually look at.
Use the prompt to build a summary tab.
Each month, paste in new data and the summary updates.
tasks.prompt: Every month I build a report from data with these columns: [list]. The numbers I need are: [list]. Give me step-by-step instructions to build a summary tab in [Excel or Google Sheets] that updates when I paste in new data. Explain each formula in plain English.

tasks.t: Cleaning up messy or duplicate data
tasks.fix: Clean the data once with clear rules, then stop the mess at the source.
steps: Copy a sample of the messy data, with personal details removed.
Use the prompt to get clean-up steps.
Add a dropdown or form so it stays clean.
tasks.prompt: Here is a sample of my messy data, with personal details removed: [paste]. Tell me what is inconsistent, then give step-by-step instructions to clean it in [Excel or Google Sheets]. Suggest one way to stop it happening again.

tasks.t: Digging through numbers to answer a question
tasks.fix: Ask your question in plain English and get the answer with the working shown.
steps: Remove personal and client details from the file.
Upload it to your AI assistant with the prompt.
Check the answer against the sheet.
tasks.prompt: I have attached a spreadsheet of [what it is]. My question: [your question]. Show how you worked out each number. If the data cannot answer the question, say so.

tasks.t: Checking one spreadsheet against another for mistakes
tasks.fix: Use a lookup formula to flag differences, then check every flag yourself.
steps: Make sure both sheets share one column, such as an invoice number.
Use the prompt to get the exact formula.
Review every flagged row by hand.
tasks.prompt: I have two sheets. Sheet A has these columns: [list]. Sheet B has: [list]. Both share [column]. Give me a formula for [Excel or Google Sheets] that flags rows that do not match, and explain it in plain English.

tasks.t: Creating and sending invoices
tasks.fix: Save your invoice details and email as a template, and repeat invoices for any regular clients.
steps: Save your standard invoice layout and payment details once.
If any clients pay the same amount regularly, check your accounting software for repeating invoices.
Save the email below as a template and send it with each invoice.
tasks.template:
Hi [name],

Please find attached invoice [number] for [amount], due on [date].

You can pay by [payment details]. If you have any questions, just reply to this email.

Thank you,
[Your name]
[Business name]

tasks.t: Chasing late payments
tasks.fix: Write your reminders once and send them on a set schedule.
steps: Check your accounting software for automatic reminders.
If it has none, use the prompt to write a set of three.
Decide at what point you pick up the phone instead.
tasks.prompt: Write three payment reminder emails for an overdue invoice: a friendly one at 7 days late, a firmer one at 14 days and a final one at 30 days. Under 80 words each. Use [invoice number], [amount] and [due date] as placeholders. Polite, never threatening.

tasks.t: Matching payments to invoices
tasks.fix: Let your bank feed suggest matches, and approve each one yourself.
steps: Check whether your accounting software has a bank feed.
Set rules for regular payments.
Approve every match yourself.
tasks.prompt: Explain in plain English how bank feeds and matching rules usually work in accounting software such as [your software], and what I should check before approving a match. Say where features may differ.

tasks.t: Collecting expense receipts
tasks.fix: Capture each receipt the day you get it, ideally with your accounting software's receipt app.
steps: Check whether your accounting software has a receipt app, and set it up on your phone.
If it has none, photograph each receipt into one shared folder the same day.
Use the prompt to set up a five-minute monthly check.
tasks.prompt: Suggest a simple routine for capturing receipts the day I get them, using [your accounting software or phone]. Include where to store them, how to name them, and a five-minute monthly check so nothing is missed.

tasks.t: Answering the same questions from new enquiries
tasks.fix: Have a ready first reply, so every new enquiry hears back the same day.
steps: List the questions new enquiries usually ask.
Save a first reply that answers them and offers a next step, such as a call.
Use the prompt for any enquiry that does not fit.
tasks.prompt: Here is a new enquiry, with personal details removed: [paste]. Draft a short first reply that thanks them, answers what they asked and offers a next step: [e.g. a call or booking link]. Under 100 words. If you need information you don't have, list it instead of guessing.

tasks.t: Following up quotes that went quiet
tasks.fix: Set a follow-up rhythm for every quote, so none go cold by accident.
steps: List your open quotes and the date each was sent.
Follow up at 3, 7 and 14 days.
Use the prompt to write the three messages once.
tasks.prompt: Write three short follow-up messages for a quote that has had no reply: one at 3 days, one at 7 days and one at 14 days. Helpful, never pushy. Under 70 words each. Use [client name], [what the quote was for] and [date sent] as placeholders.

tasks.t: Returning missed calls from potential clients
tasks.fix: Make sure every missed call gets a reply the same day.
steps: Check whether your phone system can send a text after a missed call.
Use the message below.
Set a fixed time each day to return calls. If calls come in all day, an AI phone answering service can take them for you.
tasks.template: Sorry we missed your call. We will call you back by [time]. If it is easier, book a time here: [booking link] or email [email address]. [Business name]

tasks.t: Asking happy clients for reviews
tasks.fix: Ask at the moment the client is happiest, with one link that makes it easy.
steps: Decide the moment to ask, such as when a job is signed off.
Get the direct link to your review page.
Save the message below and reuse it every time. Never offer a reward for a review.
tasks.template:
Hi [name],

Thank you for choosing us for [what we did]. If you were happy with our work, would you mind leaving a short review? It only takes a minute: [review link]

Thank you,
[Your name]
[Business name]

watch.admin-0: If you edit every template heavily each time, they are too general. Make fewer, more specific ones.
watch.admin-1: Keep a few slots free for clients who need a quick call, so the link doesn't slow down urgent work.
watch.admin-2: Don't connect tools until the manual process is clear. Automating a muddle just makes it faster.
watch.admin-3: Check names, dates and owners. AI summaries can drop or mix up actions.
watch.admin-4: A new folder system only works if everyone uses it. Agree it with the team before moving files.
watch.admin-5: Ask the person who does the job to check the checklist. AI can't know the steps people do without thinking.
watch.marketing-0: If every draft needs heavy rewriting, give the AI two of your own posts first so it learns your style.
watch.marketing-1: Ask for three versions, not thirty. Reviewing too many options costs more time than it saves.
watch.marketing-2: A reply that sounds generic can do more harm than no reply. Always add one personal detail.
watch.marketing-3: If you rewrite most of it, your notes were too thin. Add one real story or example each month.
watch.marketing-4: Small numbers can mislead. Look for patterns over a few months before changing direction.
watch.docs-0: Check every fact, date and promise. AI writes confidently even when it is guessing.
watch.docs-1: Never send a price, date or scope the AI wrote without checking it against your own notes.
watch.docs-2: Your judgement is what the client pays for. Use AI for structure, not conclusions.
watch.docs-3: Review your templates every few months, so old prices or details don't keep going out.
watch.docs-4: AI may change your meaning while fixing grammar. Read the list of changes, not just the final version.
watch.data-0: Test the form with a few real entries first, so nothing lands in the wrong column.
watch.data-1: Check the summary against one month you did by hand before you trust it.
watch.data-2: Keep a copy of the original data before cleaning, in case something is removed by mistake.
watch.data-3: AI can misread columns. Spot-check a couple of numbers against the sheet before you act.
watch.data-4: A formula only flags differences. A person still decides which version is right.
watch.paid-0: Check the invoice number, amount and due date every time. These are the details clients notice.
watch.paid-1: Automatic reminders can upset good clients. Pause them for anyone on different agreed terms.
watch.paid-2: Wrong matches can hide real problems. Never approve matches in bulk without a look.
watch.paid-3: An app only helps if you use it on the day. If receipts still pile up, the habit is the fix, not the tool.
watch.leads-0: A fast reply that misses their question loses the lead. Make sure it answers what they asked.
watch.leads-1: Stop after three follow-ups. More can damage the relationship.
watch.leads-2: Only promise a call-back time you can keep.
watch.leads-3: Never write or edit reviews for clients, and never offer rewards for them.

fitTool: What do you use for this today?

fitToolLine.email: Check what your email already offers, such as templates or rules, before adding anything new.
fitToolLine.sheet: Keep it in your spreadsheet for now. Tidy the layout first, then use the prompt with it.
fitToolLine.software: Check your software's settings first. It may already handle part of this.
fitToolLine.crm: Check your CRM or project tool first. Many have templates, reminders or automations built in.
fitToolLine.paper: Move it into one shared place first, such as a spreadsheet or shared document. That comes before any AI.
fitToolLine.nothing: Start simple. A template and a checklist come before any new tool.

fitToolPrompt.email: I currently handle this in email.
fitToolPrompt.sheet: I currently handle this in a spreadsheet.
fitToolPrompt.software: I currently handle this in accounting or booking software.
fitToolPrompt.crm: I currently handle this in a CRM or project tool.
fitToolPrompt.paper: I currently handle this with pen and paper or from memory.
fitToolPrompt.nothing: I don't use any tool for this yet.

fitHardLine.scratch: Save your best version once as a template. Next time you edit instead of write.
fitHardLine.retype: Capture it once, in one place, so nobody types it twice. A form or shared sheet often does this.
fitHardLine.waiting: Ask for everything up front with a short checklist or form, so nothing comes back half done.
fitHardLine.chasing: Write your follow-ups once and set reminders, so chasing happens on time without relying on memory.
fitHardLine.forgetting: Give it a fixed slot in your calendar with a reminder. A routine beats remembering.
fitHardLine.quality: Write down what good looks like in three points, and check every result against them before it goes out.

fitHardStep.scratch: Find your best past example and save it as your starting template.
fitHardStep.retype: Write down every place you type the same details, so you can capture them once instead.
fitHardStep.waiting: Before you start, send a short checklist of everything you need from the other person.
fitHardStep.chasing: When you send the first message, set a reminder for each follow-up so nothing relies on memory.
fitHardStep.forgetting: Book a fixed weekly slot in your calendar for this task, with a reminder.
fitHardStep.quality: Write down three things a good result must have, and check against them every time.

fitHardPrompt.scratch: I keep starting from scratch, so give me a version I can save and reuse as a template.
fitHardPrompt.retype: I keep typing the same details again, so put anything that changes in [square brackets] I can fill in quickly.
fitHardPrompt.waiting: My main difficulty is waiting on information from others. Start with a short checklist of what I should ask for up front.
fitHardPrompt.chasing: My main difficulty is chasing people. Add two short, polite follow-up messages I can send if I get no reply.
fitHardPrompt.forgetting: This task often gets left until it is late. Keep it short enough to do in one sitting and suggest a simple weekly routine.
fitHardPrompt.quality: I am never sure it is done right. End with a short checklist I can use to check the result before it goes out.
